questions.question: Compare perfect competition and monopoly in terms of demand curve, price setting, output and long-run profit, and explain verbally how each business finds its equilibrium.
questions.expected_answer: Both structures produce where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, but the demand side differs. The perfect competitor is a price taker among many sellers of a homogeneous product: its demand curve is horizontal at the market price, so D = P = AR = MR, and equilibrium is where rising marginal cost crosses that price line. Free entry and exit force long-run profit to normal: economic profit attracts entrants who compete it away, losses drive exits until survivors break even at the minimum of average cost. The monopolist is the industry: its demand curve slopes downward and marginal revenue lies below it, because selling more requires lowering the price on all units. Equilibrium output is where MC = MR, but price is read up on the demand curve above that output, so price exceeds marginal revenue, output is lower and price higher than under perfect competition. Barriers to entry — natural monopoly cost structures, licences, patents — allow economic profit to persist into the long run, though profit is not guaranteed: weak demand can leave even a monopolist making losses. Comparison essays should also touch product nature, entry, information, price control and efficiency.

questions.question: Using verbal descriptions of the relevant graphs, explain why a polluting factory and under-provision of education are both market failures, and evaluate the state's main corrective tools including maximum and minimum prices.
questions.expected_answer: The factory imposes a negative externality: the market supply curve reflects only private cost, sitting to the right of the social-cost curve that includes the harm to others, so the market equilibrium delivers too much output at too low a price; the efficient point, where social cost crosses demand, has less output at a higher price. Education carries positive externalities: private demand understates social benefit, so the social-benefit curve lies to the right of private demand and the market produces too little. Corrective tools match the failure: taxes such as fuel levies or a sugar tax shift private supply left toward the social optimum; subsidies shift demand or supply right for merit goods; the state provides public goods directly because non-rivalry and non-excludability invite free riding. Price controls carry side effects that evaluation must name: a maximum price below equilibrium keeps essentials affordable but creates a shortage with queues and black markets; a minimum price above equilibrium creates a surplus — in the labour market, a minimum wage raises the dignity and income of employed workers while pricing some job seekers out. Cost-benefit analysis disciplines big public projects by counting all social costs and benefits, proceeding only when benefits exceed costs.

questions.question: An essay asks you to discuss the measures to combat inflation in South Africa and evaluate their success. Outline the structure and content of a full-mark answer, naming the mark allocation of each part.
questions.expected_answer: Structure by the official essay grid: introduction worth a maximum of 2 marks — define inflation as a sustained and significant increase in the general price level, measured by the CPI. Main body, maximum 26 — organised by measure and linked to cause: monetary policy, where the Reserve Bank targets CPI inflation of 3 to 6 percent using the repo rate, raising it to make borrowing dearer, cool spending and anchor expectations, supported by open market transactions, cash reserve requirements and moral suasion; fiscal policy, restraining government spending and borrowing and resisting above-inflation administered price increases; and other measures such as promoting competition, raising productivity so supply grows into demand, and moderating wage settlements. Each fully explained fact in context earns two marks; bare lists earn one. Additional part, maximum 10 — the own-judgement evaluation: targeting has anchored expectations and kept South Africa clear of hyperinflation, but the repo rate fights demand-pull inflation well and cost-push badly, since higher interest rates cannot cheapen imported oil, electricity or drought-hit food, and the squeeze costs output and jobs — the Phillips curve trade-off. Conclusion, maximum 2 — a final judgement without repeating facts, for example that the mix must match the cause of the inflation. Total 40.
